claims.claim: A person grows closer to God living alone in quiet than living among other people.

stances.summary: A monk among crowds is like a fish on dry land. If we linger among people we lose our strength and forget what is within us. We must hurry back to the mountain.
stances.quote: Fishes, if they remain long on dry land, die. And so monks lose their strength if they loiter among you and spend their time with you. Wherefore as fish must hurry to the sea, so must we hasten to the mountain. Lest haply if we delay we forget the things within us.
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF Second Series vol. 4, 1892
stances.work: Life of Antony, by Athanasius of Alexandria
stances.context: Said to a military commander who begged him to stay longer; recorded by Athanasius (c. 357), who knew Antony (d. 356). The same image is a separate saying in the Sayings of the Fathers: 'As a fish when it is lifted up out of the water dieth, even so doth the monk who tarrieth outside his cell' (Budge, Paradise, Book II ch. 1 saying 20, https://www.ecatholic2000.com/athanasius/untitled-188.shtml). Antony lived about twenty years shut away (Life 14) and later fled to the 'inner mountain' because 'the multitude permit me not to be still' (Life 49). Balance: he often came down to teach and heal, and a saying credited to him in the Greek systematic collection (17.2) puts the neighbour at the centre: 'From our neighbour come life and death' (own rendering of Ἐκ τοῦ πλησίον ἡμῖν ἐστιν καὶ ἡ ζωὴ καὶ ὁ θάνατος, https://www.ldysinger.com/@texts/0400_apophth/lat_syst_w_greek/07_bk_16-18.htm). That saying is about love, not about where to live.

stances.summary: I love you, but I cannot be with God and with people at the same time. The angels have one will, people have many. So I flee from people to stay with God.
stances.quote: God knoweth that I love you, but I cannot be both with God and with men. The thousands and ten thousands of beings who are above have only one will, but men have many wills: I cannot, therefore, leave God and be with men.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (from the Syriac compilation of Anan-Isho), 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise, Book II)
stances.location: Book II, chapter 1 ('of flight from men'), saying 53; Greek alphabetical collection, Arsenius 13
stances.context: Said to Abba Macarius, who asked why he fled from the brothers. Arsenius (c. 350-445) had been a tutor at the imperial court. The same chapter records the voice he heard: 'Arsenius, flee from men, and thou shalt live' and, once a monk, 'Arsenius, flee, keep silence, and lead a life of silent contemplation, for these are the fundamental causes which prevent a man from committing sin.' He also said: 'I have many times repented that I spoke, but that I held my peace I have never repented.' Balance inside the same chapter (saying 21): an elder saw in a vision Arsenius sailing in silence with the Spirit of God, and Moses the Black, who welcomed visitors, sailing with the angels; both ways are shown as pleasing to God. Budge translates a Syriac version, so wording can differ from the Greek.

stances.summary: The one who flees from people ripens like a grape in the sun. The one who lives among people stays sour. Sit in your cell and it will teach you everything.
stances.quote: The man who fleeth from the world is like unto ripe grapes, but he who dwelleth among the attractions of the children of men is like unto sour grapes.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise, Book II)
stances.location: Book II, chapter 1, saying 35; Greek systematic collection 2.20
stances.context: Moses the Black (the Ethiopian, a former robber, d. c. 407) of Scetis. The Greek (systematic collection 2.20, as printed at https://www.ldysinger.com/@texts/0400_apophth/lat_syst_w_greek/01_Introd_bk_1-3.htm, which splits one word) reads: Ἄνθρωπος φεύγων τοὺς ἀνθρώ πους ἔοικε σταφυλῇ ὀπτῇ͵ ὁ δὲ μετὰ ἀνθρώπων ὡς ὄμφαξ ἐστίν. It says 'a man fleeing men' where Budge's Syriac-based English says 'fleeth from the world'. Also his (Greek systematic 2.19, same page): 'Go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything' (own rendering of Ὕπαγε͵ κάθου εἰς τὸ κελλίον σου καὶ τὸ κελλίον σου διδάσκει σε πάντα.). Balance: in the same Budge chapter (saying 21) Moses receives a visiting brother 'with joy' where Arsenius sat silent, and a vision approves both. He was known for hospitality and for refusing to judge others.

stances.summary: No wonder or good work in the world compares with a person sitting alone before God with full attention. Love the stillness of solitude more than feeding the hungry of the world or converting nations. Love silence above all things.
stances.quote: Compare not all powers and signs that are worked in the whole world, with a man’s consciously sitting in solitude. Love the ease of solitude rather than satisfying the hunger of the world and the converting of the multitude of heathen peoples from error unto adoring God.
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh, translated from Bedjan's Syriac text (Amsterdam: Royal Academy of Sciences), 1923
stances.work: Mystic Treatises (Ascetical Homilies), Six Treatises on the Behaviour of Excellence
stances.location: Treatise IV (Bedjan's first series, homily 4), Wensinck p. 32
stances.context: Isaac of Nineveh (7th century) was made bishop of Nineveh, resigned after about five months, and lived as a solitary in the mountains. He belonged to the Church of the East, outside the communion of Chalcedon (so formally outside the Catholic and Orthodox churches of his day), yet he is read and honoured in Orthodox tradition. He writes for monks who have chosen the solitary life; he also writes with great tenderness about mercy to every creature, so this ranking is about the solitary's calling, not contempt for charity. Also: 'Love silence above all things. It brings thee near the fruit which the tongue is too weak to interpret' (Wensinck, Treatise LXV, p. 302, same url). The url is an OCR text file; its title page OCR misreads the year as 1933, but the archive.org record of the same book gives Amsterdam 1923; Wensinck died 1939.

stances.summary: Nothing is more desirable than to shut the doors of the senses, live collected within yourself, and speak only to yourself and to God. That is how a soul becomes a clear mirror of God.
stances.quote: For nothing seemed to me so desirable as to close the doors of my senses, and, escaping from the flesh and the world, collected within myself, having no further connection than was absolutely necessary with human affairs, and speaking to myself and to God
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF Second Series vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 2, In Defence of His Flight to Pontus
stances.context: Written 362, explaining why he fled to Basil's retreat in Pontus after his father ordained him against his will. In section 6 he speaks of 'an eager longing for the blessings of calm and retirement'. He came back out of obedience and love for his people (sections 102-116), later served as bishop of Constantinople, and retired to solitude again at the end of his life. His later verdict, in the funeral oration for Basil (Oration 43.62, c. 381, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/310243.htm), is more balanced: the solitary life is 'more calm and settled, tending to union with God, yet not free from pride', and he praises Basil for uniting the solitary and the community life. He kept the preference but submitted it to duty.

stances.summary: Leave the noise of the city. Solitude calms the passions so reason can cut them out, and quiet is the first step toward holiness; a mind no longer scattered outward rises to God.
stances.quote: Now solitude is of the greatest use for this purpose, inasmuch as it stills our passions, and gives room for principle to cut them out of the soul.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, NPNF Second Series vol. 8, 1895
stances.context: EARLY VIEW, c. 358, written from his retreat on the river Iris in Pontus to invite Gregory to join him. Same section: 'Quiet, then, as I have said, is the first step in our sanctification'. The retreat was a small shared household, not a hermit's cell, and he already qualifies it: the separation that matters is 'not bodily separation, but the severance of the soul's sympathy with the body', and 'So in the end I have not got much good out of my solitude', since he carries his troubles with him (section 1). He later rejected living alone outright: see his second stance (Longer Rules 7).

stances.summary: Living alone serves only yourself and goes against the law of love. Alone you cannot practise humility, patience or mercy, and no one corrects you. Christ washed feet; alone, whose feet will you wash? Live with brothers who share your aim.
stances.quote: Whose feet then wilt thou wash ? Whom wilt thou care for? In comparison with whom wilt thou be last if thou livest by thyself?
stances.translation: W. K. L. Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (London: SPCK), 1925
stances.context: LATER VIEW, written in the 360s-370s for ascetic communities in Cappadocia; this reverses the tone of Letter 2. Clarke's heading for the question (cleaned from the OCR, which garbles its capitals): 'That it is necessary, with a view to pleasing God, to live with like-minded persons, and that solitude is difficult and dangerous.' In the same answer Basil argues that the solitary life aims only at the needs of the individual, which conflicts with the law of love; that the solitary cannot see his own faults; and that gifts of the Spirit are given for others. The url is the OCR text of the 1925 book (archive.org marks it public domain); the OCR prints a space before the first question mark ('wash ?'), and the quote copies it as it appears.

stances.summary: The desert is where God is especially present. Why stay under gloomy roofs in smoky cities? Come out to the wilderness; in spirit you will walk in paradise.
stances.quote: O wilderness, gladdened with God's special presence! What keeps you in the world, my brother, you who are above the world? How long shall gloomy roofs oppress you? How long shall smoky cities immure you?
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF Second Series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: EARLY VIEW, 373 or 374, written from the desert of Chalcis to a friend, a priest who had gone home, urging him to come back to the desert. The passage opens 'O desert, bright with the flowers of Christ!' Jerome did not last long as a hermit and later lived in a monastery at Bethlehem. In 395 he still told Paulinus: 'Forsake cities and their crowds, live on a small patch of ground, seek Christ in solitude, pray on the mount alone with Jesus', though he exempted bishops and clergy (Letter 58.4, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001058.htm). By 411 he told a young monk to live in community first: see his second stance (Letter 125).

stances.summary: I do not condemn the solitary life; I have often praised it. But no one should go into it untrained. Alone, pride creeps in. Live first in a monastery, where others teach you humility and patience.
stances.quote: What then, you will say? Do I condemn a solitary life? By no means: in fact I have often commended it. But I wish to see the monastic schools turn out soldiers who have no fear of the rough training of the desert
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF Second Series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: LATER VIEW, 411, to Rusticus, a young monk of Toulouse. The same letter keeps his old love of solitude: 'But to me a town is a prison and solitude paradise' (section 8). But he warns: 'In loneliness pride quickly creeps upon a man' (section 9), and concludes: 'Do not rely on your own discretion, but live in a monastery' (section 15). Compare Letter 14 (373-4), which urged an untrained man straight to the desert.

stances.summary: The hermit's life is the higher calling, but only after long training in community. Whoever seeks solitude just to get away from people has misunderstood it. The truly perfect person can bear both the bare desert and the weaknesses of the brothers.
stances.quote: For he is truly and not partially perfect who with equal imperturbability can put up with the squalor of the wilderness in the desert, as well as the infirmities of the brethren in the Cœnobium.
stances.translation: C. S. Gibson, NPNF Second Series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Cassian (c. 360-435) wrote the Conferences in the 420s as his own versions of the teaching of Egyptian elders, so the voice is Abbot John's but the view is Cassian's. John spent thirty years in a community and twenty as a hermit, then went back to the community. He still calls the hermit's life 'that life which can only be compared to the bliss of the angels' (19.5), but warns that untrained solitaries 'imagine that the value and the main part of this life consist in this; viz., in avoiding intercourse with the brethren and simply shunning and loathing the sight of a man' (19.10). In his own preface to Conferences 18-24 Cassian speaks of 'the sublime life of the anchorite' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/350818.htm). The page writes the word as Cœnobium in its HTML; it displays as Cœnobium.

stances.summary: The hermit's lonely fight is a true calling, but only for those tested by long life in a monastery, where the help of many has taught them. My rule is written for monks who live together.
stances.quote: Then the second kind is that of the anchorites; that is, the hermits-those who, not by the new fervour of a conversion but by the long probation of life in a monastery, have learned to fight against the devil, having already been taught by the solace of many.
stances.translation: Ernest F. Henderson, Select Historical Documents of the Middle Ages (London: George Bell and Sons, 1910), from Migne, Patrologia Latina vol. 66
stances.context: Written c. 530-540. The chapter ends by turning to 'the best kind, the cenobites' (the Latin says the strongest kind). Benedict began as a hermit himself: Gregory the Great's Life of Benedict (Dialogues Book 2, ch. 1 and 3) says he fled to a cave at Subiaco and later went back to the wilderness he loved and 'dwelt alone with himself, in the sight of his Creator' (1911 Gardner edition, https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_02_dialogues_book2.htm), before founding communities. The page prints 'hermits-those' with a hyphen where a dash is meant; copied as printed.

stances.summary: Not everyone is made for community, and not everyone for stillness. Each must know his own make. There are three ways: the lone athlete, stillness with one or two others, or patient life in community. For most, the middle way is the royal road.
stances.quote: For communities are not for everyone, because of gluttony; nor are places of stillness for everyone, because of anger; let each one look at what he is made of. The whole monastic way of life is contained in three most general states: either athletic withdrawal and solitude; or stillness with one, or at most two; or sitting patiently in a community.
stances.translation: own literal rendering from the Greek text (Migne's text as given on Greek Wikisource)
stances.original: Οὐ γὰρ πάντων τὰ κοινόβια, διὰ τὸ λιχνῶδες· οὐδὲ πάντων τὰ ἡσυχαστήρια, διὰ τὸ θυμῶδες· ἕκαστος δὲ ἐπισκέψεται ἐν ποίῳ πεποίωται. Ἐν τρισὶ γενικωτάταις καταστάσεσι καθισμάτων ἅπασα ἡ μοναχικὴ πολιτεία περιέχεται· ἢ ἐν ἀθλητικῇ ἀναχωρήσει, καὶ μονίᾳ· ἢ μετὰ ἑνὸς, ἢ πολὺ δύο ἡσυχάζειν· ἢ ἐν κοινοβίῳ ὑπομονητικῶς καθέζεσθαι.
stances.context: John Climacus (7th century) lived some forty years as a solitary near Sinai before becoming abbot of the Sinai monastery. The passage continues (same page): 'Turn not aside to the right or to the left, says Ecclesiastes, but walk the royal road; for the middle of these ways suits many', then cites 'woe to him who is alone' and 'where two or three are gathered'. In Step 27, on stillness, he rates it very high: 'I have seen those living in stillness who fed their burning desire for God through stillness without ever filling it, and begot fire from fire, love from love, and longing from longing' (own rendering of Εἶδον ἡσυχαστὰς, καὶ τὴν φλεγομένην αὐτῶν πρὸς Θεὸν ἐπιθυμίαν διὰ τῆς ἡσυχίας ἀπληρώτως πληρώσαντας· καὶ πῦρ πυρὶ, καὶ ἔρωτι ἔρωτα, καὶ πόθῳ πόθον γεννήσαντας), but also: 'Let no one troubled by anger and conceit dare to look even at a footprint of stillness' and 'Better a poor obedient monk than a distracted solitary' (own renderings; Greek at https://el.wikisource.org/wiki/%CE%9A%CE%BB%CE%AF%CE%BC%CE%B1%CE%BE/%CE%9B%CF%8C%CE%B3%CE%BF%CF%82_%CE%9A%CE%96). The only English (Moore 1959; Luibheid and Russell 1982) is copyrighted and not used.

stances.summary: The mountain does not save anyone, and the city does not damn anyone. Many hermits are lost living like townspeople, and many in cities are saved doing the desert's work. You can be alone in will among crowds, and crowded in mind when alone.
stances.quote: Many who are on the mountain have perished doing what townspeople do, and many who are in cities are saved doing the works of the desert. For it is possible to be with many and live as a solitary in one's will, and to be alone and live with crowds in one's mind.
stances.translation: own literal rendering from the Greek systematic collection of the Sayings of the Fathers
stances.original: Πολλοὶ ἐν ὄρει ὄντες τὰ τῶν δημοτῶν πράττοντες ἀπώλοντο͵ καὶ πολλοὶ ἐν πόλεσιν ὄντες τὰ τῆς ἐρήμου ἔργα ποιοῦντες σῴζονται. Δυνατὸν γὰρ μετὰ πολλῶν ὄντα μονάζειν τῇ γνώμῃ͵ καὶ μόνον ὄντα μετὰ ὄχλων τῇ διανοίᾳ διάγειν.
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), Greek systematic collection
stances.location: Greek systematic collection 2.27 (in the alphabetical collection, Syncletica 19)
stances.context: Syncletica of Alexandria (4th century) lived in seclusion outside the city and taught women who gathered to her; she valued the solitary life, so this is a warning that place alone does not make a solitary, not a rejection of solitude. ATTRIBUTION: the Latin translation of the same saying (Pelagius and John, Verba Seniorum 2.14, printed on the same page) gives it to 'abbatissa Matrona' and adds a ranking: 'Melius est enim ut cum multis sis, et solitariam vitam agas voluntate, quam cum solus sis, esse cum multitudine proposito mentis' ('it is better to be with many and live the solitary life by will than to be alone and be with the crowd in the intent of your mind'; own rendering). The Greek collections give it to Syncletica. The English printed beside the texts on that page is from modern translations and was not used.

stances.summary: Where you live is not what gives rest. Count yourself as nothing and you can live anywhere and find rest. A hundred years in a cell make no monk without humility, and a man proud of never leaving his cell should go and walk through the village.
stances.quote: If thou holdest thyself in thine own sight to be of no account, thou mayest dwell where thou pleasest, and find rest.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise, Book II)
stances.context: Poemen (Pastor, 5th century) lived as a desert monk and taught staying in the cell and silence. About a brother who boasted he had not gone into the village for years, he said: 'If I were [that man] I would go up and walk round about in the village during the night, so that my thoughts might not be able to boast themselves that I had not gone into it' (Budge, Book II ch. 8, saying 289, https://www.ecatholic2000.com/athanasius/untitled-195.shtml). And: 'If a man pass a hundred years in the cell he will not understand his departure from this world and become a monk, unless he attribute sin to himself at all times' (Budge saying 475, https://www.ecatholic2000.com/athanasius/untitled-203.shtml). The cell helps, but humility, not the place, is what counts.

stances.summary: Holy leisure with God is good and longed for, but love takes up the work others need. No one may rest in contemplation and forget his neighbour, and no one may be so busy that he forgets God.
stances.quote: No man has a right to lead such a life of contemplation as to forget in his own ease the service due to his neighbor; nor has any man a right to be so immersed in active life as to neglect the contemplation of God.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF First Series vol. 2, 1887
stances.context: Written in the 420s. Same chapter: 'holy leisure is longed for by the love of truth; but it is the necessity of love to undertake requisite business.' His own experience: 'Terrified by my sins and the load of my misery, I had resolved in my heart, and meditated flight into the wilderness; but You forbade me' (Confessions 10.43.70, c. 400, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/110110.htm). To monks on an island he wrote that they pray 'more lively and undistracted' than busy clergy, yet 'Do not prefer your own ease to the claims of the Church' (Letter 48, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102048.htm). He always lived in community, never as a hermit.

stances.summary: In the quiet of the monastery I was near God; now, busy with the world, I feel banished from His face. Yet a gifted person who hides in quiet instead of serving others is guilty before God.
stances.quote: For I have lost the deep joys of my quiet, and seem to have risen outwardly while inwardly falling down. Whence I grieve to find myself banished far from the face of my Maker.
stances.translation: James Barmby, NPNF Second Series vol. 12, 1895
stances.context: Written 591, just after he was made pope against his wishes. He felt solitude brought him nearer to God, but he taught that love obliges the gifted to serve. In the Pastoral Rule (1.5, c. 590-591) he judges gifted people who 'love a secret place of quiet' and 'long for a retreat for speculation' instead of serving: 'they are, if strictly judged, undoubtedly guilty in proportion to the greatness of the gifts whereby they might have been publicly useful' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/36011.htm). In the Dialogues (Book 1, preface, 593) he mourns his lost monastic rest and says very many 'in a contemplative and retired kind of life, much please God' (1911 Gardner edition, https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_01_dialogues_book1.htm).

stances.summary: The public life of the clergy and the hidden life of the monk are both excellent. The monk's life is safer; the one who lives in the open arena meets more temptations and so wins the greater victory.
stances.quote: the one endures more frequent temptations, and so has the greater victory, the other falls less often, and keeps guard more easily.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, NPNF Second Series vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: Letter 63, to the Church of Vercelli
stances.context: Written c. 396. 'The one' is the public life of the clergy, 'the other' the monk's retired life; the section opens: 'The one then contends, the other retires; the one overcomes incitements, the other flees from them'. In 63.71 he calls both 'the most excellent' in Christian devotion, and in 63.72: 'the one was more agreeable, the other more safe'. He praises Eusebius of Vercelli for joining the two, and notes that Elijah and John the Baptist were trained in solitude before their public work (63.75-76).

stances.summary: Holiness depends on what you do, not where you are. A monk made bishop can even grow better by serving his people. Yet the desert life of Antony deserves all honour.
stances.quote: But let a man, wherever he is, strive earnestly; for the crown is given not according to position, but according to action.
stances.translation: Archibald Robertson, NPNF Second Series vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: Written 354 or 355 to a monk and abbot who hid to avoid being made a bishop; monks had advised him that the office would make him worse. Athanasius answers: 'while before your election you lived to yourself, after it, you live for your flock' (section 2) and 'you may even grow better if you imitate Paul' (section 8). In his Life of Antony (c. 357) he praises Antony's withdrawal and tells how 'the desert was colonised by monks' (ch. 14, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/2811.htm). So he honoured the solitary life but denied that it is holier than serving people. The tilt of this letter is toward disagree.

stances.summary: Living alone keeps you safe, but it proves little: a helmsman in harbour shows no skill. The greater virtue is to stay pure while living among many and serving them. No one is saved who does not work for the salvation of others.
stances.quote: But if any one admire a solitary life, and retirement from the society of the multitude, I should say myself that such a life was a token of patience, but not a sufficient proof of entire fortitude of soul. For the man who sits at the helm in harbor, does not yet give any certain proof of his art.
stances.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF First Series vol. 9, 1889
stances.context: Written c. 386-390, a dialogue with his friend Basil (not Basil the Great). As a young man Chrysostom lived as a monk in the hills near Antioch, the last two years alone in a cave, until his health broke (reported by Palladius; not checked here), and his early treatise Against the Opponents of the Monastic Life (c. 378) defends the monks (no public-domain English found). Here he says he would 'vote a thousand times over' to excel in church oversight rather than in the recluse's life (6.7), and: 'I am not myself able to believe that it is possible for one who has not labored for the salvation of his fellow to be saved' (6.10). He admits he keeps to his cell because his soul is weak (6.12). Later sermons admire the desert monks (Homily 68 on Matthew) yet urge that 'the self-denial that is practised in the deserts, let us bring into our cities' (Homily 55 on Matthew, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200155.htm), and 'nothing can so make a man an imitator of Christ as caring for his neighbors' (Homily 25 on 1 Corinthians, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220125.htm).

stances.summary: No one should walk the road of the ascetic life alone. Find a guide who has lived it. Alone, a person is easily beaten on the way to God, and has no one to lift him up.
stances.quote: a single one is easily vanquished by the foe who infests the path which leads to God; and verily woe to him that is alone when he falls, for he has not another to help him up.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF Second Series vol. 5, 1893
stances.context: Written c. 371. The sentence begins 'Two are better than one, says the Preacher'. The chapter is about the need for a living teacher and warns against self-taught zealots whose pride 'had a shocking fall'; it is not a full argument about hermits. Weak evidence on the exact claim, but a clear voice against going it alone.

stances.summary: The single man who cares only for himself is spared temptation, and that proves little. The greater person keeps close to God's love while caring for a wife, children and a household.
stances.quote: one is not really shown to be a man in the choice of single life; but he surpasses men, who, disciplined by marriage, procreation of children, and care for the house, without pleasure or pain, in his solicitude for the house has been inseparable from God's love
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 200, before monasticism. The contrast is single life versus family life, not desert versus city, but the principle matches the claim: 'Caring, then, for himself alone, he is surpassed by him who is inferior, as far as his own personal salvation is concerned, but who is superior in the conduct of life'. Clement does not reject solitude: the true Christian honours God 'in every place, even if he be alone by himself' (7.7).

stances.summary: God made us social so that we would help one another. Our first duty is to God and our second to people. Whoever cuts himself off from human society lives like a wild beast.
stances.quote: But he who withdraws and separates himself from the body at large, must live not after the custom of men, but after the manner of wild beasts. But if this cannot be done, the bond of human society is by all means to be retained, because man can in no way live without man.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Written c. 303-311, before monasticism. The target is those who refuse to give or receive help, especially philosophers who strip away mercy, not Christian hermits. Same chapter: 'For God, since He is kind, wished us to be a social animal.' Evidence on the exact claim is indirect.

stances.summary: Pray with the whole Church. If the prayer of two has power, the prayer of the gathered Church has far more. Whoever keeps apart from the assembly shows his pride.
stances.quote: He, therefore, that does not assemble with the Church, has even by this manifested his pride, and condemned himself.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 107-110 on the way to martyrdom. He addresses Christians who stayed away from the common Eucharist under the bishop; hermits did not yet exist. Chapter 13: 'For when you assemble frequently in the same place, the powers of Satan are destroyed'. Indirect evidence on the claim: it is about worship, not where one lives.

stances.summary: Christians do not flee human life to live in the woods. We live among our neighbours, work and trade with them, and thank God for all He made.
stances.quote: We are not Indian Brahmins or Gymnosophists, who dwell in woods and exile themselves from ordinary human life. We do not forget the debt of gratitude we owe to God, our Lord and Creator; we reject no creature of His hands
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.context: Written 197, before his Montanist years, answering the charge that Christians are useless to society; it is partly a defence, but it describes how Christians lived. Later, in On the Pallium (c. 205-209), the philosopher's cloak speaks for him: 'I have withdrawn from the populace. My only business is with myself' and 'The better life you would more enjoy in seclusion than in publicity' (ANF vol. 4, https://www.tertullian.org/anf/anf04/anf04-03.htm). That piece is ironic and concerns public office, not nearness to God, so it is noted here rather than counted as a change of mind. Weak evidence on the exact claim.

stances.summary: As a monk alone I had more of God's power than as a bishop among the crowds. So even as bishop he made a hidden retreat outside the city to live as a hermit.
stances.quote: Martin was accustomed to say to you, that such an abundance of power was by no means granted him while he was a bishop, as he remembered to have possessed before he obtained that office.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF Second Series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Sulpicius knew Martin (d. 397). Here Gallus, Martin's disciple, speaks to Sulpicius in a literary dialogue (c. 404), so Martin's words are reported, not quoted; the 'power' meant is the power to work miracles. In the Life of Martin (ch. 10) Sulpicius says that as bishop Martin could not bear the crowds visiting his cell by the church and founded Marmoutier two miles away, a place 'so secret and retired that he enjoyed in it the solitude of a hermit' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3501.htm). He still served actively as bishop.

stances.summary: Those who go to lonely places are not mad or savage. They turn their eyes to God, love a rest free of empty cares, and flee the din of public life for Christ's sake and their salvation.
stances.quote: they love repose void of empty cares, and shun the din of public life, the bustle of affairs, and all concerns hostile to the gifts of Heaven both by Christ's command and in desire for salvation.
stances.translation: H. G. Evelyn White, Ausonius, with an English translation (Loeb Classical Library), vol. 2, 1921
stances.original: otia amant strepitumque fori rerumque tumultus cunctaque divinis inimica negotia donis, et Christi imperiis et amore salutis, abhorrent
stances.location: Carmen 10, lines 156-168 (printed in the Loeb Ausonius as Epistle 31)
stances.context: Written c. 393-394 to his old teacher Ausonius, who accused him of hiding in the wilds. Paulinus (c. 354-431), a wealthy senator, gave up his fortune and withdrew with his wife Therasia to Nola, living an ascetic life at the shrine of St Felix and receiving pilgrims; he later became bishop there. He is defending those who live in lonely places, and denies being a hermit himself: 'my mind does not wander, nor even does my life flee from intercourse with men'. So he stands for withdrawal from public life for God, not for living alone. The url is an OCR text file of the Loeb volume.

stances.summary: Flee from people. And when there is nowhere farther to flee, flee by silence: go into your cell, shut the door and sit.
stances.quote: Then Macarius laid his hand upon his mouth, saying, “Flee in this manner,” and straightway he went to his cell and, shutting the door, sat down.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise, Book II)
stances.context: Macarius of Egypt (the Great, c. 300-390), a founder of Scetis. After the church service he told the brothers 'Flee ye, O brethren'; an elder asked where they could flee beyond the desert. NOT in the candidate pool; recorded for completeness.

stances.summary: Even to think of the freedom of the desert is better than living anywhere else.
stances.quote: Are not the mere thoughts of the freedom which is in the desert better for us [than living out of it]?
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise, Book II)
stances.context: Sisoes (d. c. 429), who lived on Antony's mountain, was grieved at having to leave the desert in old age; said to Abba Ammon. The bracketed words are Budge's addition. NOT in the candidate pool; recorded for completeness.

splits_fathers: Real voices on both sides, and a large middle. Clearly for: the desert fathers of Egypt (Antony, Arsenius, Moses the Black, Macarius, Sisoes), Isaac the Syrian, Gregory of Nazianzus, the young Jerome and the young Basil, and in practice Martin of Tours and Paulinus of Nola. Clearly against: Basil in his Longer Rules (alone, whose feet will you wash?) and John Chrysostom in On the Priesthood (solitude is a harbour, not a test of skill); before monasticism existed, Clement, Lactantius, Tertullian and Ignatius assume or argue that the Christian life is lived among people. Most later teachers take a deliberate middle: solitude is the higher or sweeter life, but only after long training in community, and love may call a person out of it (Cassian, Benedict, the older Jerome, John Climacus, Augustine, Gregory the Great, Ambrose, Athanasius). The desert itself also taught that the place matters less than humility and the inner life (Syncletica, Poemen). Two people changed their minds on record (Basil, Jerome), and Augustine says he wanted to flee to the desert but God forbade him. Among monastic writers of the 4th to 7th centuries the majority rank solitude as the higher calling for the few; community became the norm for the many, in the East after Basil and in the West after Benedict.
splits_people_today: A genuine split, so the item discriminates. Many people, religious or not, say they feel closest to God (or to something larger than themselves) alone: in nature, on retreat, in silent prayer. Introverts, contemplatives and many 'spiritual but not religious' people lean agree. Most churchgoing Christians, especially in evangelical, Catholic parish and Orthodox parish settings, are taught that faith is lived in community and that God is met in the neighbour, and would lean disagree; extroverts too. Temperament will drive many answers, which suits a personality-flavoured quiz but means the item partly measures introversion. Wording caution for the quiz writer: 'living alone' can be read today as a household arrangement (a single person living alone), which is not what the Fathers meant; their question is withdrawal into quiet versus a life lived among and for other people.

misattributions.line: Arsenius, flee, be silent, pray always, for these are the source of sinlessness
misattributions.truth: Garbled. These are words Arsenius heard from a voice, not his own advice, and the third verb is not 'pray': the Greek is Ἀρσένιε͵ φεῦγε͵ σιώπα͵ ἡσύχαζε͵ αὗται γάρ εἰσιν αἱ ῥίζαι τῆς ἀναμαρτησίας. ('Arsenius, flee, be silent, be still, for these are the roots of sinlessness', own rendering), the Latin 'fuge, tace, quiesce' ( Greek systematic collection 2.4, Latin Verba Seniorum 2.3, both at https://www.ldysinger.com/@texts/0400_apophth/lat_syst_w_greek/01_Introd_bk_1-3.htm). Budge's Syriac-based 1907 English reads 'Arsenius, flee, keep silence, and lead a life of silent contemplation'.

misattributions.line: Many who live in the mountains ... it is possible to be a solitary in one's mind while living in a crowd
misattributions.truth: The Greek alphabetical and systematic collections give it to Syncletica, but the Latin Verba Seniorum (Pelagius and John 2.14) gives it to 'abbatissa Matrona'. Safe to cite as Syncletica from the Greek, with that caveat.
Pseudonymous; a 5th-century text transmitted under Athanasius's name. Do not use it as Syncletica's own words without that caveat.

misattributions.line: The Sayings chapter 'of flight from men' in Budge's Paradise, Book II
misattributions.attributed_to: Palladius (Budge's chapter heading says 'Composed by Bishop Palladius for the Prefect Lausus'); the ecatholic2000 site files the whole Paradise under 'Saint Athanasius of Alexandria'
misattributions.truth: These are sayings from the Apophthegmata (Sayings of the Desert Fathers) in the 7th-century Syriac compilation of Anan-Isho, translated by Budge (1907). Palladius wrote the Lausiac History, and Athanasius only the Life of Antony in volume 1. Cite the sayings as Sayings of the Fathers, by the abba named.

misattributions.line: A monk is one who is separated from all and united to all
misattributions.attributed_to: St Nilus of Sinai / Nilus of Ancyra (as printed in the Philokalia and Migne)
misattributions.truth: From Evagrius Ponticus, On Prayer 124; the treatise was handed down under the name of Nilus. Not verified against a public-domain text in this research.

misattributions.line: Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh ... 1933
misattributions.attributed_to: the OCR title page of the archive.org scan
misattributions.truth: OCR error in the scan; the book is Wensinck's 1923 Amsterdam edition (the archive.org record of another copy says 'Published in Amsterdam in 1923').

notes: Best pairs for the reveal: Arsenius ('I cannot be both with God and with men') against Basil (whose feet will you wash if you live alone?); Antony's fish on dry land against Chrysostom's helmsman in harbour; Syncletica (a person can be a solitary in will among crowds) as the middle. Isaac the Syrian is the most extreme agree voice (solitude over feeding the hungry); Lactantius the most extreme disagree voice (the one who withdraws lives like a wild beast), though his target is not hermits. Two recorded changes of mind: Basil (Letter 2, c. 358, then Longer Rules 7) and Jerome (Letter 14, 373-4, then Letter 125, 411); each has two stances. Gregory the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus felt one way and did another out of duty; Augustine says he planned to flee to the desert and God forbade him (Confessions 10.43). Pre-monastic writers (Ignatius, Clement, Tertullian, Lactantius) never address hermits; their stances are strength 1 and indirect. Budge's Paradise translates a Syriac version of the Sayings, so wording can differ from the Greek (Moses: 'fleeth from the world' vs Greek 'fleeing men'). Modern English versions of the Sayings (Ward 1975, Waddell 1936), of Climacus (Moore 1959, Luibheid and Russell 1982), and of Chrysostom's Against the Opponents of the Monastic Life (Hunter 1988) are copyrighted and were not used; the ldysinger pages print modern English beside the Greek and Latin, and only the Greek and Latin were taken from them. Not recorded as stances: Evagrius (no verifiable public-domain text found for On Prayer 124; the Evagrius lines in Budge are quoted second-hand inside a later question-and-answer section); Cyprian (On the Lord's Prayer 4 praises prayer 'in hidden and remote places', and 8 calls prayer 'public and common', but it is about prayer, not about where to live); Chrysostom's line about praying that the need for monasteries would pass (Against the Opponents, only in copyrighted English; not checked in the Greek). Other relevant voices not in the pool and not researched: Pachomius, Hilarion, Paul of Thebes, Theodore of Pherme. One more desert story useful as colour (Budge Book II ch. 1 saying 24): Abba Apos lost his former grace after becoming bishop of Oxyrhynchus and was told: 'formerly thou wast in the desert, and there were no men there, and God took care of thee; here, however, thou art in a portion of the world which is inhabited, and men care for thee.' The candidate pool has no clear voice on this topic for Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen, Perpetua, Hippolytus, Novatian, Hilary, Ephrem, Macrina, Pelagius or Boethius.
